q: Is coastal shipping lower carbon than road freight within India?
title: Coastal shipping or road freight?
short: Per tonne-km a coastal ship is usually far below a truck, but door to door it depends on the route. Sea distances around the coast are often longer than the highway, and trucks still haul to and from both ports. Work out the break-even sea factor for your lane and compare.
audience: Shippers moving bulk and containers between Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and the east coast

sections.h: Three things that decide the answer
ul: Sea distance against road distance. Gujarat to Tamil Nadu by sea goes round the peninsula and can be longer than the highway.
Port drayage: the truck legs from your plant to the load port and from the discharge port to the customer, at the truck's per tonne-km factor.
Vessel type and size. Small coastal feeders and general cargo ships have higher factors per tonne-km than large ocean vessels, so do not borrow a deep-sea container figure for a coastal leg.

sections.h: How to compute it door to door
ol: Road only: tonnes x road km x the truck class factor.
Coastal: tonnes x drayage km x truck factor, plus tonnes x sea km x the vessel factor, for each leg.
Add port handling at each port if the operator reports it; ISO 14083 counts hub emissions as part of the chain.
Compare totals on the same basis, well-to-wheel CO2e per the GLEC Framework, and name the edition of the defaults.

p: Subtract the drayage emissions from the road-only total and divide what is left by the sea tonne-km. That is the highest vessel factor at which coastal still wins. If the GLEC default or the operator's figure for your vessel is well below it, coastal is lower carbon. If it is close, the answer turns on load factor and port handling, and it is not a safe claim.

Long lanes with ports close to both ends, such as plant and customer each within a few dozen kilometres of a port, and full shipments of bulk or containers. Short lanes with long drayage at both ends rarely gain much, and part loads on a small vessel can lose to a full tractor-trailer.

example.title: Worked example: break-even for a 40 t load (illustrative distances)
lines: Road only: 40 t x 2,000 km = 80,000 tonne-km x 0.0551 (tractor-trailer) = 4,408 kg CO2e
Coastal drayage: 40 t x (50 + 50) km = 4,000 tonne-km x 0.0551 = 220.4 kg CO2e
Left for the sea leg: 4,408 minus 220.4 = 4,187.6 kg CO2e
Sea leg: 40 t x 2,600 km = 1,04,000 tonne-km
Break-even vessel factor: 4,187.6 / 1,04,000 = 0.0403 kg CO2e per tonne-km
Decision: coastal wins only if the vessel's factor, plus port handling, is below about 0.040
example.note: 0.0551 is the default for a 30 to 60 t GVW tractor-trailer in India. Take the vessel factor from the GLEC defaults for your ship type and size.
